query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A carefully tailored annealing treatment that selectively recrystallizes the ductile phase within the dual-phase lamellar structure will alleviate dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries, thereby reducing stress concentrations and preventing microcracking, while maintaining or boosting the strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies, where a hard phase coexists with a softer phase that has not been recrystallized, resulting in pronounced dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries and limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply a phase-selective annealing treatment—using a specific temperature-time profile (e.g., around 700°C for a short duration) after deformation processing—to trigger full recrystallization of the ductile phase while retaining the integrity of the hard phase.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under standard conditions; the annealing process must be optimized to preferentially recrystallize only the soft phase without causing significant coarsening or undesirable phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure transforms from an inhomogeneous dual-phase lamellar arrangement with problematic, unrecrystallized interfaces to one where a fully recrystallized ductile phase is embedded in a continuous hard-phase network.
generation.mechanism: Selective recrystallization relieves local dislocation accumulation by enabling uniform deformation in the soft phase, which in turn prevents dislocation pile-ups at the phase boundaries. This alleviates local stress concentrations that would otherwise lead to microcrack initiation and catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in tensile ductility (e.g., achieving an elongation to failure of around 35%) while retaining or even enhancing yield and ultimate tensile strength (targeting around 2 GPa true stress) compared to the untreated alloy that typically shows only ~8–14% elongation.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness due to dislocation accumulation and stress concentration at the internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention relies on precise control of the annealing parameters; if the temperature or duration is too high, it may lead to undesired coarsening or phase changes, which would compromise the balance of strength and ductility.
generation.uncertainty: Exact annealing conditions may need fine tuning based on the specific alloy composition and prior deformation history. Quantitative improvements in ductility and strength may vary and require validation for each batch of material.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic HEA batch. Subject one set to the proposed phase-selective annealing treatment and leave the second set as a control. Characterize both sets via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to determine the extent of selective recrystallization. Conduct room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both groups.
measurements: Grain size and phase distribution using TEM/EBSD
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and percentage elongation from tensile tests
Dislocation density near phase boundaries via high-resolution TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples fail to show a clear microstructural transition with selective recrystallization of the soft phase (i.e., similar dislocation pile-up and interface characteristics as the control) or if the mechanical tests do not show a significant improvement in ductility (e.g., elongation remaining ~8–14%) while maintaining strength, then the hypothesis is falsified.

A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing

Abstract: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. Hierarchical Eutectoid Nano-lamellar Decomposition in an Al0.3CoFeNi Complex Concentrated Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThis paper reports a novel eutectoid nano-lamellar (FCC + L12)/(BCC + B2) microstructure that has been discovered in a relatively simple Al0.3CoFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) or complex concentrated alloy (CCA). This novel eutectoid nano-lamellar microstructure presumably results from the complex interplay between Al-mediated lattice distortion (due to its larger atomic radius) in a face-centered cubic (FCC) CoFeNi solid solution, and a chemical ordering tendency leading to precipitation of ordered phases such as L12 and B2. This eutectoid microstructure is a result of solid-state decomposition of the FCC matrix and therefore distinct from the commonly reported eutectic microstructure in HEAs which results from solidification. This novel nano-lamellar microstructure exhibits a tensile yield strength of 1074 MPa with a reasonable ductility of 8%. The same alloy can be tuned to form a more damage-tolerant FCC + B2 microstructure, retaining high tensile yield stress (~900 MPa) with appreciable tensile ductility (>20%), via annealing at 700 °C.
